claim: Six tau isoforms that range from 352 to 441 amino acids in length are expressed in adult human brain from a single gene by alternative mRNA splicing.
source: Six tau isoforms that range from 352 to 441 amino acids in length are expressed in adult human brain from a single gene by alternative mRNA splicing (Goedert et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goedert et al., 1989.

claim: The tau sequence can be separated into an N-terminal projection domain (residues 1–150), a proline-rich region (residues 151–243), the microtubule-binding repeat region (residues 244–368), and a C-terminal domain (residues 369–441).
source: The tau sequence can be separated into an N-terminal projection domain (residues 1–150), a proline-rich region (residues 151–243), the microtubule-binding repeat region (residues 244–368), and a C-terminal domain (residues 369–441).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about tau protein structure.

claim: Tau isoforms differ by the presence or absence of 1 or 2 inserts of 29 amino acids each in the N-terminal region (0N, 1N or 2N).
source: Isoforms differ by the presence or absence of 1 or 2 inserts of 29 amino acids each, in the N-terminal region (0N, 1N or 2N), and the presence or absence of the second of four microtubule-binding repeats of 31 or 32 amino acids each (resulting in three-repeat, 3R, and four-repeat, 4R, isoforms).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau isoform structure.

claim: Tau isoforms differ by the presence or absence of the second of four microtubule-binding repeats of 31 or 32 amino acids each (resulting in three-repeat, 3R, and four-repeat, 4R, isoforms).
source: Isoforms differ by the presence or absence of 1 or 2 inserts of 29 amino acids each, in the N-terminal region (0N, 1N or 2N), and the presence or absence of the second of four microtubule-binding repeats of 31 or 32 amino acids each (resulting in three-repeat, 3R, and four-repeat, 4R, isoforms).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau isoform structure.

claim: The second N-terminal insert is only expressed together with the first.
source: The second N-terminal insert is only expressed together with the first.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau isoform expression.

claim: A mixture of all six tau isoforms is present in the tau filaments of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Thus, a mixture of all six isoforms is present in the tau filaments of Alzheimer's disease (AD), chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), and other diseases; in Pick's disease (PiD), filaments are composed of only 3R tau isoforms; and in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal degeneration (CBD), globular glial tauopathy (GGT), argyrophilic grain disease (AGD), and other tauopathies, filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau filament composition in AD, supported by the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: A mixture of all six tau isoforms is present in the tau filaments of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).
source: Thus, a mixture of all six isoforms is present in the tau filaments of Alzheimer's disease (AD), chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), and other diseases; in Pick's disease (PiD), filaments are composed of only 3R tau isoforms; and in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal degeneration (CBD), globular glial tauopathy (GGT), argyrophilic grain disease (AGD), and other tauopathies, filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau filament composition in CTE.

claim: In Pick's disease (PiD), tau filaments are composed of only 3R tau isoforms.
source: Thus, a mixture of all six isoforms is present in the tau filaments of Alzheimer's disease (AD), chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), and other diseases; in Pick's disease (PiD), filaments are composed of only 3R tau isoforms; and in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal degeneration (CBD), globular glial tauopathy (GGT), argyrophilic grain disease (AGD), and other tauopathies, filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau filament composition in PiD.

claim: In progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), tau filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
source: Thus, a mixture of all six isoforms is present in the tau filaments of Alzheimer's disease (AD), chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), and other diseases; in Pick's disease (PiD), filaments are composed of only 3R tau isoforms; and in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal degeneration (CBD), globular glial tauopathy (GGT), argyrophilic grain disease (AGD), and other tauopathies, filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau filament composition in PSP.

claim: In corticobasal degeneration (CBD), tau filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
source: Thus, a mixture of all six isoforms is present in the tau filaments of Alzheimer's disease (AD), chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), and other diseases; in Pick's disease (PiD), filaments are composed of only 3R tau isoforms; and in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal degeneration (CBD), globular glial tauopathy (GGT), argyrophilic grain disease (AGD), and other tauopathies, filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau filament composition in CBD.

claim: In globular glial tauopathy (GGT), tau filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
source: Thus, a mixture of all six isoforms is present in the tau filaments of Alzheimer's disease (AD), chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), and other diseases; in Pick's disease (PiD), filaments are composed of only 3R tau isoforms; and in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal degeneration (CBD), globular glial tauopathy (GGT), argyrophilic grain disease (AGD), and other tauopathies, filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau filament composition in GGT.

claim: In argyrophilic grain disease (AGD), tau filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
source: Thus, a mixture of all six isoforms is present in the tau filaments of Alzheimer's disease (AD), chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), and other diseases; in Pick's disease (PiD), filaments are composed of only 3R tau isoforms; and in progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal degeneration (CBD), globular glial tauopathy (GGT), argyrophilic grain disease (AGD), and other tauopathies, filaments are composed of only 4R tau isoforms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau filament composition in AGD.

claim: Tau filaments consist of a structured core made mostly of the repeat domain, with less structured N- and C-terminal regions forming the fuzzy coat.
source: Tau filaments consist of a structured core made mostly of the repeat domain, with less structured N- and C-terminal regions forming the fuzzy coat (Goedert et al., 1988; Wischik et al., 1988a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goedert et al., 1988 and Wischik et al., 1988a.

claim: Electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) has been used to determine the atomic structures of the cores of tau filaments extracted from the brains of individuals with a number of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Previously, we and others used electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) to determine the atomic structures of the cores of tau filaments extracted from the brains of individuals with a number of neurodegenerative diseases (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017; Falcon et al., 2018a; Falcon et al., 2019; Falcon et al., 2019; Arakhamia et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Tau filaments from different individuals with a given disease share the same structures.
source: Whereas, tau filaments from different individuals with a given disease share the same structures, different diseases tend to be characterised by distinct tau folds.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior cryo-EM studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Different diseases tend to be characterised by distinct tau folds.
source: Whereas, tau filaments from different individuals with a given disease share the same structures, different diseases tend to be characterised by distinct tau folds.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior cryo-EM studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Identical tau protofilaments can arrange in different ways to give rise to distinct filaments (ultrastructural polymorphs).
source: Identical protofilaments can arrange in different ways to give rise to distinct filaments (ultrastructural polymorphs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau filament structure.

claim: In AD, two protofilaments can combine in a symmetrical way to form paired helical filaments (PHFs).
source: In AD, two protofilaments can combine in a symmetrical way to form paired helical filaments (PHFs), or in an asymmetrical manner to form straight filaments (SFs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD tau filament structure.

claim: In AD, two protofilaments can combine in an asymmetrical manner to form straight filaments (SFs).
source: In AD, two protofilaments can combine in a symmetrical way to form paired helical filaments (PHFs), or in an asymmetrical manner to form straight filaments (SFs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD tau filament structure.

claim: The extent of the ordered cores of the protofilament folds explains the isoform composition of tau filaments.
source: The extent of the ordered cores of the protofilament folds explains the isoform composition of tau filaments.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Alzheimer and CTE folds consist almost entirely of R3 and R4.
source: Alzheimer and CTE folds consist almost entirely of R3 and R4; the Pick fold comprises most of R1, as well as all of R3 and R4; and the CBD, PSP, GGT, and AGD folds comprise the whole of R2, R3, and R4.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: The Pick fold comprises most of R1, as well as all of R3 and R4.
source: Alzheimer and CTE folds consist almost entirely of R3 and R4; the Pick fold comprises most of R1, as well as all of R3 and R4; and the CBD, PSP, GGT, and AGD folds comprise the whole of R2, R3, and R4.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: The CBD, PSP, GGT, and AGD folds comprise the whole of R2, R3, and R4.
source: Alzheimer and CTE folds consist almost entirely of R3 and R4; the Pick fold comprises most of R1, as well as all of R3 and R4; and the CBD, PSP, GGT, and AGD folds comprise the whole of R2, R3, and R4.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: All known tau folds contain residues 369–379/380 from the C-terminal domain.
source: All known tau folds also contain residues 369–379/380 from the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: A hierarchical classification of tauopathies has been proposed based on tau fold structures.
source: Based on these findings, we proposed a hierarchical classification of tauopathies, which complements clinical and neuropathological characterisation, and allows identification of new disease entities (Shi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2021.

claim: In human diseases, full-length tau assembles into filaments intracellularly.
source: In human diseases, full-length tau assembles into filaments intracellularly (Goedert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goedert et al., 2017.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of the fuzzy coat is characteristic of extracellular ghost tangles.
source: Proteolytic cleavage of the fuzzy coat is characteristic of extracellular ghost tangles (Endoh et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Endoh et al., 1993.

claim: Full-length recombinant tau is highly soluble.
source: Yet, full-length recombinant tau is highly soluble and in vitro assembly into filaments requires the addition of anionic co-factors, such as sulphated glycosaminoglycans, RNA, fatty acids, and polyglutamate (Goedert et al., 1996; Kampers et al., 1996; Pérez et al., 1996; Wilson and Binder, 1997; Friedhoff et al., 1998) or the use of harsh shaking conditions with small beads and sodium azide (Chakraborty et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about recombinant tau properties.

claim: In vitro assembly of full-length recombinant tau into filaments requires the addition of anionic co-factors, such as sulphated glycosaminoglycans, RNA, fatty acids, and polyglutamate.
source: Yet, full-length recombinant tau is highly soluble and in vitro assembly into filaments requires the addition of anionic co-factors, such as sulphated glycosaminoglycans, RNA, fatty acids, and polyglutamate (Goedert et al., 1996; Kampers et al., 1996; Pérez et al., 1996; Wilson and Binder, 1997; Friedhoff et al., 1998) or the use of harsh shaking conditions with small beads and sodium azide (Chakraborty et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In vitro assembly of full-length recombinant tau into filaments can be achieved using harsh shaking conditions with small beads and sodium azide.
source: Yet, full-length recombinant tau is highly soluble and in vitro assembly into filaments requires the addition of anionic co-factors, such as sulphated glycosaminoglycans, RNA, fatty acids, and polyglutamate (Goedert et al., 1996; Kampers et al., 1996; Pérez et al., 1996; Wilson and Binder, 1997; Friedhoff et al., 1998) or the use of harsh shaking conditions with small beads and sodium azide (Chakraborty et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chakraborty et al., 2021.

claim: The addition of heparin to full-length 3R or 4R recombinant tau expressed in Escherichia coli led to the formation of polymorphic filaments with structures unlike those in disease.
source: We previously showed that the addition of heparin to full-length 3R or 4R recombinant tau expressed in Escherichia coli led to the formation of polymorphic filaments, with structures that are unlike those in disease (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: The addition of RNA to full-length recombinant 4R tau led to filament structures that are different from those observed in disease thus far.
source: Below, we showed that the addition of RNA or phosphoserine to full-length recombinant 4R tau also led to filament structures that are different from those observed in disease thus far.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The addition of phosphoserine to full-length recombinant 4R tau led to filament structures that are different from those observed in disease thus far.
source: Below, we showed that the addition of RNA or phosphoserine to full-length recombinant 4R tau also led to filament structures that are different from those observed in disease thus far.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Templated seeding, where filaments provide a template for the incorporation of tau monomers, underlies the hypothesis of prion-like spreading of tau pathology.
source: The mechanisms of templated seeding, where filaments provide a template for the incorporation of tau monomers, thus resulting in filament growth, underlies the hypothesis of prion-like spreading of tau pathology.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau pathology mechanisms.

claim: Protein misfolding cyclic amplification (PMCA) and real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) are commonly used techniques for seeded assembly.
source: Protein misfolding cyclic amplification (PMCA) and real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) are commonly used (Soto et al., 2002; Saijo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Soto et al., 2002 and Saijo et al., 2020.

claim: PMCA and RT-QuIC may not always amplify the predominant filamentous assemblies.
source: However, they may not always amplify the predominant filamentous assemblies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the need for structural verification mentioned in the text.

claim: For α-synuclein and immunoglobulin light-chain, cryo-EM has shown that using similar amplification methods, the structures of seeded filaments differed from those of the seeds under the conditions used.
source: For α-synuclein and immunoglobulin light-chain, cryo-EM has shown that using similar amplification methods, the structures of seeded filaments differed from those of the seeds under the conditions used (Burger et al., 2021; Lövestam et al., 2021; Radamaker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burger et al., 2021; Lövestam et al., 2021; and Radamaker et al., 2021.

claim: A fragment consisting of residues 250–378, excluding R2, formed filaments when using the hanging drop approach.
source: A fragment consisting of residues 250–378, excluding R2, formed filaments when using the hanging drop approach, a method commonly used in protein crystallography (Crowther et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Crowther et al., 1992.

claim: K11 and K12 constructs (tau residues 244–394 for K11, and the same sequences, excluding R2, for K12) formed filaments.
source: The same was true of K11 and K12 constructs (tau residues 244–394 for K11, and the same sequences, excluding R2, for K12) (Wille et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wille et al., 1992.

claim: Proteins comprising the ordered cores of tau filaments from AD [residues 306–378], PiD [residues 254–378, but excluding R2], and CBD [residues 274–380] have been reported to assemble into filaments.
source: Moreover, proteins comprising the ordered cores of tau filaments from AD [residues 306–378], PiD [residues 254–378, but excluding R2], and CBD [residues 274–380] have been reported to assemble into filaments (Carlomagno et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carlomagno et al., 2021.

claim: Constructs K18 and K19, which comprise the microtubule-binding repeats and four amino acids after the repeats (residues 244–372 for K18, and the same sequences, excluding R2, for K19), spontaneously assemble into filaments.
source: Multiple studies have also used constructs K18 and K19, which comprise the microtubule-binding repeats and four amino acids after the repeats (residues 244–372 for K18, and the same sequences, excluding R2, for K19); they spontaneously assemble into filaments (Gustke et al., 1994; Mukrasch et al., 2005; von Bergen et al., 2006; Li et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2012; Shammas, 2015) and are seeding-active by RT-QuIC (Saijo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: K18 and K19 constructs are seeding-active by RT-QuIC.
source: Multiple studies have also used constructs K18 and K19, which comprise the microtubule-binding repeats and four amino acids after the repeats (residues 244–372 for K18, and the same sequences, excluding R2, for K19); they spontaneously assemble into filaments (Gustke et al., 1994; Mukrasch et al., 2005; von Bergen et al., 2006; Li et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2012; Shammas, 2015) and are seeding-active by RT-QuIC (Saijo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saijo et al., 2020.

claim: Since all known tau structures from human brain include residues beyond 372, tau filament structures of K18 and K19 cannot be the same as those in disease.
source: However, since all known tau structures from human brain include residues beyond 372, tau filament structures of K18 and K19 cannot be the same as those in disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural knowledge.

claim: dGAE comprises residues 297–391 of 4R tau and was identified as the proteolytically stable core of PHFs from tangle fragments of AD.
source: Another fragment that has been used for in vitro assembly studies is dGAE, which comprises residues 297–391 of 4R tau, and was identified as the proteolytically stable core of PHFs from tangle fragments of AD (Wischik et al., 1988b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wischik et al., 1988b.

claim: dGAE assembles into filaments with similar morphologies to AD PHFs by negative staining EM and atomic force microscopy.
source: It assembles into filaments with similar morphologies to AD PHFs by negative staining EM and atomic force microscopy (Novak et al., 1993; Al-Hilaly et al., 2017; Al-Hilaly et al., 2020; Lutter et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Conditions have been identified that lead to the formation of AD PHFs from purified tau (297–391) expressed in E. coli.
source: Here, we report conditions that lead to the formation of AD PHFs from purified tau (297–391) expressed in E. coli.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: The same tau (297–391) construct can be used to form type II filaments of CTE.
source: We show that the same construct can also be used to form type II filaments of CTE, and demonstrate how different cations affect the differences between the structures of the two diseases.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: Different cations affect the differences between the structures of AD and CTE filaments.
source: We show that the same construct can also be used to form type II filaments of CTE, and demonstrate how different cations affect the differences between the structures of the two diseases.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: 76 cryo-EM structures have been reported, including those of 27 previously unobserved filaments.
source: We report 76 cryo-EM structures, including those of 27 previously unobserved filaments.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: In vitro assembly of tau (297–391) in 10 mM phosphate buffer containing 10 mM dithiothreitol, with shaking at 700 rpm, led to filament formation within 4 hr.
source: We first performed in vitro assembly of tau (297–391) in 10 mM phosphate buffer (PB) containing 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), with shaking at 700 rpm, as described (Al-Hilaly et al., 2017). We will refer to this as assembly condition 1. Filaments formed within 4 hr, as indicated by ThT fluorescence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Cryo-EM imaging after 48 hr of assembly condition 1 revealed a single type of filament comprising two protofilaments that were related by pseudo-21 helical screw symmetry.
source: Cryo-EM imaging after 48 hr revealed a single type of filament comprising two protofilaments that were related by pseudo-21 helical screw symmetry.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data in the manuscript.

claim: The extent and topology of the ordered cores of filaments from assembly condition 1 resembled those of the protofilaments of AD and CTE, but the protofilament cores were extended, rather than C-shaped.
source: Although the extent and topology of the ordered cores resembled those of the protofilaments of AD and CTE, the protofilament cores were extended, rather than C-shaped (Figure 2A–C; filament type 1a).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and structural analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Reducing the shaking speed to 200 rpm resulted in a slower assembly reaction, with filaments appearing after 6 hr.
source: We then reduced the shaking speed to 200 rpm. This resulted in a slower assembly reaction, with filaments appearing after 6 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Cryo-EM structure determination after 48 hr at 200 rpm shaking showed that the filaments were polymorphic and shared the AD protofilament fold, spanning residues 305–378.
source: Cryo-EM structure determination after 48 hr showed that the filaments were polymorphic. They shared the AD protofilament fold, spanning residues 305–378.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data in the manuscript.

claim: Besides AD PHFs, filaments comprising three or four protofilaments, called triple helical filaments (THFs) and quadruple helical filaments (QHFs), were observed at 200 rpm shaking.
source: However, besides AD PHFs, we also observed filaments comprising three or four protofilaments, which we called triple helical filaments (THFs) and quadruple helical filaments (QHFs) (Figure 2D; filament types 2b–d).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: THFs and QHFs have not been observed in brain extracts from individuals with AD.
source: THFs and QHFs have not been observed in brain extracts from individuals with AD (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017; Falcon et al., 2018b), possibly because the presence of the fuzzy coat would hinder their formation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: THFs consist of a PHF and an additional single protofilament with the AD fold.
source: THFs consist of a PHF and an additional single protofilament with the AD fold, whereas QHFs are made of two stacked PHFs that come in two different arrangements (types 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural analysis in the manuscript.

claim: QHFs are made of two stacked PHFs that come in two different arrangements (types 1 and 2).
source: THFs consist of a PHF and an additional single protofilament with the AD fold, whereas QHFs are made of two stacked PHFs that come in two different arrangements (types 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural analysis in the manuscript.

claim: The addition of 200 mM MgCl2, 20 mM CaCl2, or 0.1 μg/ml dextran sulphate resulted in purer populations of PHFs (~95%).
source: In particular, the addition of 200 mM MgCl2, 20 mM CaCl2, or 0.1 μg/ml dextran sulphate resulted in purer populations of PHFs (~95%) (Figure 2E; filament types 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cryo-EM structure determination of filaments made using MgCl2, CaCl2, or dextran sulphate confirmed that their ordered cores were identical, with a root mean square deviation (r.m.s.d) of all non-hydrogen atoms of 1.3 Å, to those of AD PHFs.
source: Cryo-EM structure determination of filaments made using these conditions confirmed that their ordered cores were identical, with a root mean square deviation (r.m.s.d) of all non-hydrogen atoms of 1.3 Å, to those of AD PHFs (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and structural comparison shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Assembly of tau (266–391), excluding R2, in the presence of 200 mM MgCl2 gave rise to AD PHFs with a purity greater than 94%.
source: We also assembled tau (266–391), excluding R2, in the presence of 200 mM MgCl2, as well as a 50:50 mixture of the 3R/4R tau constructs, in the absence of MgCl2. We observed PHFs, THFs, and QHFs in the absence of MgCl2, whereas assembly in the presence of 200 mM MgCl2 gave rise to AD PHFs with a purity greater than 94% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; filament types 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bona fide PHFs can be formed from only 3R or 4R, albeit truncated, tau.
source: These findings show that bona fide PHFs can be formed from only 3R or 4R, albeit truncated, tau.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing PHF formation from 3R or 4R constructs.

claim: The cryo-EM structures of in vitro assembled PHFs and of AD PHFs shared the same left-handed twist and pseudo-21 helical screw symmetry.
source: The cryo-EM structures of in vitro assembled PHFs and of AD PHFs shared the same left-handed twist and pseudo-21 helical screw symmetry.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural analysis in the manuscript.

claim: There were similar additional densities in front of lysine residues 317 and 321, and on the inside of the protofilament's C, in both in vitro assembled PHFs and AD PHFs.
source: Moreover, there were similar additional densities in front of lysine residues 317 and 321, and on the inside of the protofilament's C, as we previously observed for AD PHFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The additional densities in in vitro assembled PHFs likely arose from phosphate ions in the buffer.
source: Although we cannot exclude the possibility that negatively charged co-factors may have purified together with recombinant tau, it appears more likely that the additional densities arose from phosphate ions in the buffer.
evidence: This is speculation based on the composition of the assembly buffer.

claim: Addition of ZnCl2 resulted in the same fold as observed for filaments assembled using condition 1.
source: Addition of ZnCl2 resulted in the same fold as observed for filaments assembled using condition 1, whereas addition of CuCl2 led to folds with little resemblance to previously observed tau folds (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; filament types 11 and 12).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of CuCl2 led to folds with little resemblance to previously observed tau folds.
source: Addition of ZnCl2 resulted in the same fold as observed for filaments assembled using condition 1, whereas addition of CuCl2 led to folds with little resemblance to previously observed tau folds (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1; filament types 11 and 12).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cu2+ ions led to the formation of intermolecular disulphide bonds that were part of the ordered cores of filaments.
source: Cu2+ ions led to the formation of intermolecular disulphide bonds that were part of the ordered cores of these filaments.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis of filaments formed with CuCl2.

claim: Addition of 200 mM NaCl led to the formation of two types of filaments: one identical to CTE type II filaments and another with a previously unobserved, extended protofilament fold.
source: Addition of 200 mM NaCl led to the formation of two types of filaments. The first type was identical, with an all-atom r.m.s.d. of 1.4 Å to CTE type II filaments (Figure 3A–C; filament type 8a); in the second type (filament type 8b), two identical protofilaments with a previously unobserved, extended protofilament fold packed against each other with pseudo-21 helical symmetry.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3.

claim: When adding 200 mM LiCl, two types of filaments were observed, with either C-shaped or more extended protofilament folds.
source: When adding 200 mM LiCl, we observed two types of filaments, with either C-shaped or more extended protofilament folds (Figure 3A; filament types 10a and 10b).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Addition of 200 mM KCl led to two different filaments with either extended or C-shaped protofilament folds.
source: Addition of 200 mM KCl also led to two different filaments with either extended or C-shaped protofilament folds. However, in this case, low numbers of filaments with extended protofilaments resulted in poor cryo-EM reconstructions. The filaments with C-shaped folds comprised three protofilaments, which packed against each other with C3 symmetry (Figure 1; Figure 3A; filament type 10a).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 3A.

claim: For each monovalent cation, residues 338–354 adopted identical conformations when comparing extended and C-shaped protofilament folds.
source: For each monovalent cation, residues 338–354 adopted identical conformations when comparing extended and C-shaped protofilament folds (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The 1.9 Å cryo-EM reconstruction of the threefold symmetric filaments formed with KCl showed two spherical blobs of additional density per β-rung that were 3.1 Å apart.
source: The cryo-EM reconstructions of the threefold symmetric filaments formed with KCl, with a resolution of 1.9 Å, showed multiple additional spherical densities inside the protofilament core. Besides additional densities for what were probably water molecules in front of several asparagines and glutamines, the cavity at the tip of the fold contained two larger, separate spherical densities per β-rung, which were 3.1 Å apart, and at approximately 3.0–4.5 Å distance from S341 and S352, the only polar residues in the cavity.
evidence: This is supported by high-resolution cryo-EM data.

claim: The additional densities in the cavity of filaments formed with KCl likely correspond to pairs of K+ and Cl− ions.
source: Below, we will argue that these densities corresponded to pairs of K+ and Cl− ions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the size, shape, and position of the densities.

claim: The additional density in filaments formed with NaCl may correspond to Na+ and Cl− ions.
source: Therefore, it is possible that the extra density in the cavity of filaments formed with NaCl also corresponds to Na+ and Cl− ions.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with KCl filaments.

claim: The observation that filaments formed with NaCl are identical to CTE type II filaments suggests that the cavity in CTE filaments may contain NaCl.
source: The observation that the filaments formed with NaCl are identical to CTE type II filaments, which show a similar extra density, suggests that, rather than being filled with hydrophobic co-factors, the cavity in CTE filaments may contain NaCl.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural similarity between in vitro NaCl filaments and CTE filaments.

claim: Proteins comprising the entire N-terminal domain (residues 1–391 of 0N4R tau) did not assemble into filaments.
source: Proteins comprising the entire N-terminal domain (residues 1–391 of 0N4R tau) did not assemble into filaments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Proteins starting at residues 151, 181, or 231 in the proline-rich region did not assemble into filaments.
source: The same was true of proteins starting at residues 151, 181, or 231 in the proline-rich region.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: When using proteins starting at 244, the first residue of R1, filaments were observed.
source: When using proteins starting at 244, the first residue of R1, we observed the formation of filaments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Proteins that started at residues 258 or 266 in R1 formed PHFs.
source: However, it is possible that this construct will form filaments with the Alzheimer fold after further optimisation of assembly conditions. Proteins that started at residues 258 or 266 in R1 formed PHFs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Tau (297–391) can be shortened from the N-terminus, as proteins starting at residues 300 or 303 still formed filaments with AD or CTE folds.
source: Tau (297–391) can also be shortened from the N-terminus, as proteins starting at residues 300 or 303 still formed filaments with AD or CTE folds (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; filament types 25–26).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When shortened to residue 306, filaments were observed, but their stickiness precluded cryo-EM structure determination.
source: When shortened to residue 306, we also observed filaments, but their stickiness precluded cryo-EM structure determination.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: No filaments were formed when shortening the protein to residue 310.
source: No filaments were formed when shortening the protein to residue 310.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The PHF6 motif (306VQIVYK311 in tau) is essential for filament formation.
source: It has previously been shown that the PHF6 motif (306VQIVYK311 in tau) is essential for filament formation (von Bergen et al., 2000; Li and Lee, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to von Bergen et al., 2000 and Li and Lee, 2006.

claim: Tau starting at residue 297 and ending at 441 failed to assemble into filaments.
source: Reminiscent of what we observed for the N-terminal domain, the tau starting at residue 297 and ending at 441 failed to assemble into filaments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Tau (297–431) failed to assemble into filaments.
source: The same was true of tau (297–431).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Proteins ending at residues 421, 412, 402, or 396 formed filaments, but their ordered cores are much smaller than in the Alzheimer fold.
source: However, proteins ending at residues 421, 412, 402, or 396 formed filaments, but their ordered cores are much smaller than in the Alzheimer fold, precluding cryo-EM structure determination to sufficient resolution for unambiguous atomic modelling (Figure 4B; filament types 28–31).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Filaments with the Alzheimer fold were observed for a protein ending at residue 394.
source: We did observe filaments with the Alzheimer fold for a protein ending at residue 394 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 4B; filament type 32).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4B.

claim: When tau (297-391) was shortened from the C-terminus to residue 384, it could still form AD and CTE folds.
source: As observed for proteins ending at residue 384, when tau (297-391) was shortened from the C-terminus, it could still form AD and CTE folds (Figure 4B; filament type 33).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Constructs ending at residue 380 formed straight ribbons, precluding cryo-EM structure determination.
source: However, constructs ending at residue 380 formed straight ribbons, precluding cryo-EM structure determination.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Reducing the shaking speed from 700 to 200 rpm was important for the formation of filaments with the AD fold by tau (297–391).
source: As shown in Figure 2, we found that reducing the shaking speed from 700 to 200 rpm was important for the formation of filaments with the AD fold by tau (297–391).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When assembling tau (258–391) at 700 rpm, protofilaments with partial similarity to the GGT fold were observed.
source: When assembling tau (258–391) at 700 rpm, we observed protofilaments with partial similarity to the GGT fold. The structures were nearly identical at residues 288–322, with an all-atom r.m.s.d. of 1.5 Å, (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; filament type 38a).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The absence of a non-proteinaceous co-factor may have precluded formation of bona fide GGT filaments.
source: It is possible that the absence of a non-proteinaceous co-factor, which was hypothesised to be present inside the GGT fold, precluded formation of bona fide GGT filaments.
evidence: This is speculation based on the partial similarity to GGT folds.

claim: Addition of heparan sulphate or phosphoglycerate to the assembly buffer did not result in formation of the GGT fold.
source: Addition of heparan sulphate or phosphoglycerate to the assembly buffer did not result in formation of the GGT fold (Figure 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; filament types 39–41).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In vitro filament assembly of recombinant tau repeats was inhibited by N- and C-terminal regions.
source: Whereas in vitro filament assembly of recombinant tau repeats was inhibited by N- and C-terminal regions, it is predominantly or only full-length tau that assembles into filaments in AD (Lee et al., 1991; Goedert et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citations to Lee et al., 1991 and Goedert et al., 1992.

claim: It is predominantly or only full-length tau that assembles into filaments in AD.
source: Whereas in vitro filament assembly of recombinant tau repeats was inhibited by N- and C-terminal regions, it is predominantly or only full-length tau that assembles into filaments in AD (Lee et al., 1991; Goedert et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 1991 and Goedert et al., 1992.

claim: Tau undergoes extensive post-translational modifications in AD.
source: This difference may be due to the fact that we used unmodified recombinant proteins for in vitro assembly, while tau undergoes extensive post-translational modifications in AD (Wesseling et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wesseling et al., 2020.

claim: Immunochemistry and mass spectrometry have identified abnormal hyperphosphorylation of S396, S400, T403, and S404 in PHF-tau.
source: Immunochemistry and mass spectrometry have identified abnormal hyperphosphorylation of S396, S400, T403, and S404 in PHF-tau (Lee et al., 1991; Hasegawa et al., 1992; Kanemaru et al., 1992; Morishima-Kawashima et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Phosphorylation of S396, S400, T403, and S404 may modulate PHF formation and help to overcome the inhibitory effects of the C-terminal domain.
source: Because these sites are located in the C-terminal domain that prevents the formation of PHFs from recombinant tau, we hypothesised that their phosphorylation may modulate PHF formation and help to overcome the inhibitory effects of the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the location of phosphorylation sites.

claim: Tau (297–408) with four phospho-mimetic mutations (S396D, S400D, T403D, S404D) formed two types of filaments consisting of AD PHF protofilaments.
source: As described above, tau (297–408) formed filaments with small ordered cores; its pseudophosphorylated mutant formed two types of filaments consisting of AD PHF protofilaments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Tau (297–441), which does not assemble into filaments, did so in presence of the four phospho-mimetic mutations.
source: Importantly, tau (297–441), which does not assemble into filaments, did so in presence of the four phospho-mimetic mutations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Filaments of tau (297–441) with four phospho-mimetic mutations consisted of a single protofilament with the AD fold.
source: Filaments consisted of a single protofilament with the AD fold.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural analysis in the manuscript.

claim: AD filaments may be phosphorylated at S356.
source: It has been suggested that AD filaments may also be phosphorylated at S356 (Hanger et al., 1998; Hanger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hanger et al., 1998 and Hanger et al., 2007.

claim: Using tau (266–391) with S356D, PHFs were not formed; instead, filaments consisted of two asymmetric protofilaments with features reminiscent of the GGT fold.
source: However, using tau (266–391) with S356D, we were unable to form PHFs. Instead, filaments consisted of two asymmetric protofilaments, both of which had features reminiscent of the GGT fold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: In the presence of NaCl, tau (266–391) with S356D formed filaments with a novel fold, consisting of two identical protofilaments related by pseudo-21 helical symmetry.
source: In the presence of NaCl, this construct formed filaments with a novel fold, consisting of two identical protofilaments related by pseudo-21 helical symmetry (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; filament types 44 and 45).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of RNA to full-length tau led to the formation of two asymmetrical and extended protofilaments, similar to heparin-induced 3R tau filaments.
source: Addition of RNA led to the formation of two asymmetrical and extended protofilaments, similar to heparin-induced 3R tau filaments (Zhang et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; filament type 46).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: A 1.8 Å resolution reconstruction was calculated for full-length tau filaments that formed in the presence of 5 mM phosphoserine.
source: We calculated a 1.8 Å resolution reconstruction for full-length tau filaments that formed in the presence of 5 mM phosphoserine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; filament type 47).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphoserine-induced filaments are right-handed.
source: At this resolution, the absolute handedness of the filament was obvious from the position of the main-chain carbonyl oxygens. Whereas most tau filaments described in this paper have a left-handed twist (see Methods), phosphoserine-induced filaments are right-handed.
evidence: This is supported by high-resolution cryo-EM data.

claim: The ordered core of phosphoserine-induced filaments comprised residues 375–441, encompassing only residues from the C-terminal domain.
source: Surprisingly, the ordered core of this filament comprised residues 375–441, encompassing only residues from the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural analysis.

claim: Phosphoserine-induced filaments consist of two protofilaments that are related by pseudo-21 helical symmetry.
source: Filaments consist of two protofilaments that are related by pseudo-21 helical symmetry and the protofilament fold contains eight β-strands.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural analysis.

claim: This is the first example of a region outside the microtubule-binding repeats of tau forming amyloid filaments.
source: This is the first example of a region outside the microtubule-binding repeats of tau forming amyloid filaments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural finding that the C-terminal domain forms the ordered core.

claim: The observation that same proteins can adopt multiple different amyloid structures challenges the paradigm by which a protein's sequence defines its structure.
source: The observation that same proteins can adopt multiple different amyloid structures has made it clear that the paradigm by which a protein's sequence defines its structure may not hold for amyloids.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural diversity observed for tau and other amyloid proteins.

claim: The packing of β-sheets against each other in amyloid filaments can happen in many ways for a single amino acid sequence.
source: Apparently, the packing of β-sheets against each other in amyloid filaments can happen in many ways for a single amino acid sequence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural diversity observed.

claim: Similar observations of structural diversity have been made for amyloid-β.
source: Similar observations have been made for amyloid-β (Bertini et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2013; Xiao et al., 2015; Wälti et al., 2016; Kollmer et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2022), α-synuclein (Tuttle et al., 2016; Li et al., 2018a; Li et al., 2018b; Guerrero-Ferreira et al., 2019; Schweighauser et al., 2020; Lövestam et al., 2021), TAR DNA binding protein-43 (Arseni et al., 2022; Li et al., 2021), and immunoglobulin light chain (Radamaker et al., 2019; Swuec et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on other amyloid proteins.

claim: For tau, the different amyloid structures define distinct neurodegenerative conditions.
source: However, the observation that, for tau, and possibly also other proteins, the different amyloid structures define distinct neurodegenerative conditions, raises important questions on what drives their formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: The lack of in vitro assembly models for recombinant tau that replicates the amyloid structures observed in disease has hampered progress.
source: The lack of in vitro assembly models for recombinant tau that replicates the amyloid structures observed in disease has hampered progress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the need for better model systems.

claim: Conditions for the in vitro assembly of AD PHFs and type II CTE filaments have been identified.
source: Here, we identified conditions for the in vitro assembly of AD PHFs and type II CTE filaments and established the formation of these structures by cryo-EM structure determination to resolutions sufficient for atomic modelling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: The ability to make AD PHFs and CTE type II filaments in vitro opens new avenues for studying tauopathies.
source: The ability to make AD PHFs and CTE type II filaments in vitro opens new avenues for studying tauopathies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the potential applications of the in vitro assembly system.

claim: In vitro assembly assays could be used to screen for compounds that inhibit filament formation.
source: In vitro assembly assays could be used to screen for compounds that inhibit filament formation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the in vitro assembly system.

claim: In vitro generated filaments may be used in high-throughput screens for small-molecule compounds or biologics that bind specifically to a single type of filament.
source: Alternatively, in vitro generated filaments may be used in high-throughput screens for small-molecule compounds or biologics that bind specifically to a single type of filament.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the in vitro assembly system.

claim: Amyloid structure-specific binders could be developed into ligands for positron emission tomography to differentiate between tauopathies in living patients.
source: Such amyloid structure-specific binders could be developed into ligands for positron emission tomography to differentiate between tauopathies in living patients.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of structure-specific binders.

claim: Specific binders could be explored for use in therapeutic approaches that aim to degrade filaments inside neurons through their coupling with the protein degradation machinery inside the cell.
source: Moreover, specific binders could be explored for use in therapeutic approaches that aim to degrade filaments inside neurons through their coupling with the protein degradation machinery inside the cell.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: Post-translational modifications of tau may lead to a higher propensity to form amyloid filaments in disease.
source: It is therefore possible that post-translational modifications of tau lead to a higher propensity to form amyloid filaments in disease.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings with phospho-mimetic mutations.

claim: The enzymes causing post-translational modifications of tau could be therapeutic targets.
source: Thus, the enzymes causing these modifications could be therapeutic targets.
evidence: This is speculation based on the potential role of post-translational modifications in filament formation.

claim: Most of the structures share features with the Alzheimer and CTE folds: a cross-β packing of residues from near the start of R3 against residues from near the start of the C-terminal domain, and a turn in R4.
source: Moreover, most of the structures in Figure 1, all of which are of recombinant tau proteins over-expressed in E. coli, share features with the Alzheimer and CTE folds: a cross-β packing of residues from near the start of R3 against residues from near the start of the C-terminal domain, and a turn in R4.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Unmodified tau may have a tendency to form filaments that resemble Alzheimer and CTE folds.
source: Unmodified tau may have a tendency to form filaments that resemble Alzheimer and CTE folds, whereas specific post-translational modifications and/or associated molecules may play a role in driving the formation of tau folds associated with other tauopathies.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: Specific post-translational modifications and/or associated molecules may play a role in driving the formation of tau folds associated with other tauopathies.
source: Unmodified tau may have a tendency to form filaments that resemble Alzheimer and CTE folds, whereas specific post-translational modifications and/or associated molecules may play a role in driving the formation of tau folds associated with other tauopathies.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural observations.
